lead: A spark-ignition (SI) engine burns a fuel–air mixture that was mixed before the spark. The spark starts a small flame at the plug, the flame grows into a thin front that sweeps across the chamber, and the last pockets of charge burn slowly during expansion. Textbooks split this into three stages: ignition lag, flame propagation and afterburning. You see all three on the cylinder pressure–crank angle (p–θ) diagram, and that diagram is how engineers set spark timing and judge whether combustion is healthy.
prereq: You need: the four-stroke cycle, top dead centre (TDC) and crank angle, and how the spark is timed (ignition systems).

sections.h3: The three stages on the p–θ diagram

blocks.text: Plot cylinder pressure p against crank angle θ, measured from TDC, with angles before TDC (bTDC) negative. Draw two curves: the firing curve with combustion, and the motoring curve, the pressure when the engine is turned over with no combustion. The gap between them is the pressure that combustion adds. Three points mark the stages.

items: A, the spark. The spark jumps at a set angle before TDC, for example 28° bTDC.

B, first pressure rise. The firing curve leaves the motoring curve. Between A and B lies stage I, the ignition lag (some books call it the preparation phase). A small flame kernel forms and grows around the plug gap, but it is too small to move the pressure.

C, peak pressure. Between B and C lies stage II, flame propagation. The flame front sweeps the chamber and burns most of the charge, so pressure climbs steeply even though the piston has started down.
After C comes stage III, afterburning. The charge near the walls, in crevices and behind the front finishes burning while the gas expands, so the curve falls.

blocks.text: Ignition lag is a chemical and physical delay: radicals must build up and the kernel must grow before burning becomes self-sustaining. It lasts about 1 to 2 ms in a normal engine. It is shortest near the chemically correct, slightly rich mixture and becomes longer with lean mixtures, residual exhaust gas, low temperature and a weak spark.

sections.h3: Flame propagation and the mass burned

blocks.text: Once the kernel is about a few millimetres across, a flame front grows out of it. The front is a thin reaction zone, from a fraction of a millimetre to about a millimetre thick, with burnt gas behind it and fresh charge ahead. Turbulence wrinkles the front, which raises its area and the rate at which it eats into the fresh charge.

The burnt gas is three to four times less dense than the unburnt charge at the same pressure. So the burning gas expands, pushes the unburnt charge ahead of it and squeezes it. This squeezing is why the last charge to burn, the end gas, gets hot before the flame reaches it; that matters for knock (see abnormal combustion).

Laboratory engines describe the burn by the mass fraction burned xb, from 0 at the spark to 1 at the end. Two angles summarise it: the flame development angle, spark to 10 % burned, which matches stage I and the start of stage II; and the rapid burning angle, 10 % to 90 % burned, which is the bulk of stage II. Peak pressure normally falls at about 12° to 18° after TDC (aTDC); a peak much earlier means too much spark advance, much later means too little.

sections.h3: Why spark advance must change with speed

blocks.text: Ignition lag is roughly a fixed time, in milliseconds, set by chemistry. Flame propagation, in contrast, speeds up almost in proportion to engine speed, because the turbulence that drives it scales with piston speed. So stage II takes about the same number of crank degrees at any speed, but stage I takes more degrees as the engine runs faster.

To keep peak pressure near 15° aTDC, the spark must therefore be advanced as speed rises. That is the job of the spark advance map in the engine control unit, and of the centrifugal advance in older distributors (see ignition timing and spark advance). Load matters too: at part throttle the charge is thinner and diluted by more residual gas, the lag grows, and the spark is advanced further.

Read the three stages as a checklist when an engine runs badly. A long lag points to a weak spark, a lean mixture or heavy dilution. Slow propagation puts the peak late and loses work. Heavy afterburning raises the exhaust temperature and the unburnt hydrocarbons. Flame speed and the slope of the pressure rise are taken up in flame velocity and rate of pressure rise.

examples.question: An SI engine (bore 86 mm, stroke 86 mm, compression ratio 9) runs at 3000 rev/min with the spark at 28° bTDC. The ignition lag is 1.0 ms. The measured trace peaks at 50.3 bar at 15.6° aTDC. (a) Find the lag in crank degrees and the angle at which pressure first rises. (b) Find the duration of flame propagation in degrees and in milliseconds. (c) At 4500 rev/min the lag is still 1.0 ms and stage II still ends at 15.6° aTDC. What spark timing keeps the first pressure rise at the same angle?
steps: Start the count at the spark: −28° + 18° = −10°. Pressure first rises at 10° bTDC (point B).
At 4500 rev/min: 0.006 × 4500 = 27 °/ms, so the same 1.0 ms lag is 27°.
For B to stay at −10°, the spark must be at −10° − 27° = −37°, that is 37° bTDC: 9° more advance than at 3000 rev/min.
Check: −37° + 27° = −10°, the same point B as before.
examples.answer: (a) 18° of lag; pressure first rises at 10° bTDC. (b) Flame propagation lasts 25.6°, or 1.42 ms. (c) Advance the spark to 37° bTDC.

traps: The motoring curve is the pressure with no combustion (the engine turned over with the ignition off). Do not call it "the curve with fuel but no spark"; fuel has nothing to do with its definition.
Stage I ends at point B, where the firing curve leaves the motoring curve, not when the flame reaches the cylinder wall.
In the three-stage picture, flame propagation ends at peak pressure (point C). Do not put peak pressure at the end of afterburning.
Crank degrees and milliseconds are different units. A 1.0 ms lag is 18° at 3000 rev/min and 27° at 4500 rev/min.
Advancing the spark does not shorten the lag in milliseconds; it starts the same lag earlier so that point B stays where it should.

quiz.q: Name the three stages of SI combustion in order and the points on the p–θ diagram that separate them.
quiz.a: Ignition lag (spark A to first pressure rise B), flame propagation (B to peak pressure C), afterburning (after C).
The cylinder pressure against crank angle when the engine is driven round with no combustion. The firing curve is compared with it to find where combustion starts adding pressure.

quiz.q: Why must the spark be advanced as engine speed rises?
quiz.a: Ignition lag is roughly a fixed time. At higher speed that time covers more crank degrees, while flame propagation keeps about the same degrees because turbulence rises with speed. So the spark must fire earlier to keep peak pressure near 15° aTDC.

quiz.q: Why does the end gas heat up before the flame reaches it?
quiz.a: Burnt gas is much less dense than unburnt charge, so it expands and compresses the unburnt charge ahead of the front; the rising piston adds to this before TDC.

quiz.q: At 2000 rev/min the lag is 1.2 ms and the spark fires at 12° bTDC. Find the lag in degrees and the angle of first pressure rise.
A trace at 3000 rev/min has its 10 % burned point at 0° and its 90 % burned point at 17° aTDC. Find the rapid burning angle in degrees and milliseconds.
A trace leaves the motoring curve at 4° aTDC and peaks at 28° aTDC. What do you conclude, and what two causes would you check?
quiz.a: The burn starts and peaks late, so work is lost and exhaust temperature rises. Check spark timing (too retarded) and a long lag from a lean or heavily diluted mixture or a weak spark.

quiz.q: A student says the flame propagation stage is unimportant because it lasts only about 1.4 ms. Do you agree?
quiz.a: No. Stage II burns most of the charge and gives almost all of the pressure rise and work; its length in degrees decides where peak pressure falls. Its short time is exactly why the timing must be right.

beyond: Production engines hold the 50 % burned point near 8° to 10° aTDC with knock and ion-current feedback, and laboratory engines fit the mass fraction burned with the Wiebe function to compare designs. Optical engines film the flame kernel and show how it wrinkles in the first millisecond. Search for mass fraction burned, Wiebe function and combustion phasing (CA50).

figure.caption: The worked example’s engine at 3000 rev/min: the spark at A (28° bTDC) is followed by 18° of ignition lag until the trace leaves the motoring curve at B (10° bTDC); flame propagation then lifts the pressure to its peak at C, and afterburning follows as the gas expands.

spec.aria: Cylinder pressure against crank angle from 40 degrees before to 60 degrees after top dead centre. The motoring curve peaks at about 19 bar at TDC. The firing curve leaves it at 10 degrees before TDC and peaks at 50.3 bar at 15.6 degrees after TDC. Shaded bands mark ignition lag from the spark at 28 degrees before TDC, flame propagation, and afterburning.
